Topics · Who was Muhammad?

Why does the Quran correct its own Prophet?

The Quran records him frowning at a blind man, questions a decision, calls him human. And it is still recited.

Part 1 of 3

﴿بِسْمِ ٱللَّهِ ٱلرَّحْمَـٰنِ ٱلرَّحِيمِ عَبَسَ وَتَوَلَّىٰٓ١ أَن جَآءَهُ ٱلْأَعْمَىٰ٢ وَمَا يُدْرِيكَ لَعَلَّهُۥ يَزَّكَّىٰٓ٣ أَوْ يَذَّكَّرُ فَتَنفَعَهُ ٱلذِّكْرَىٰٓ٤ أَمَّا مَنِ ٱسْتَغْنَىٰ٥ فَأَنتَ لَهُۥ تَصَدَّىٰ٦ وَمَا عَلَيْكَ أَلَّا يَزَّكَّىٰ٧ وَأَمَّا مَن جَآءَكَ يَسْعَىٰ٨ وَهُوَ يَخْشَىٰ٩ فَأَنتَ عَنْهُ تَلَهَّىٰ١٠﴾

Translation of the meaning

He [i.e., the Prophet (ﷺ) ] frowned and turned away Because there came to him the blind man,[1853] [interrupting]. But what would make you perceive, [O Muḥammad], that perhaps he might be purified[1854] Or be reminded and the remembrance would benefit him? As for he who thinks himself without need,[1855] To him you give attention. And not upon you [is any blame] if he will not be purified.[1856] But as for he who came to you striving [for knowledge] While he fears [Allāh], From him you are distracted.

Translator's notes

[1853] ʿAbdullāh, the son of Umm Maktūm.

[1854] As a result of what he learns from you.

[1855] i.e., without need of faith or need of Allāh (subḥānahu wa taʿālā) . Here it is in reference to a certain influential member of the Quraysh whom the Prophet (ﷺ) had hoped to bring to Islām.

[1856] The Prophet (ﷺ) was responsible only for conveying the message, not for ultimate guidance.

Quran · Abasa 80:1-10

Translation

“‘You shall not curse the deaf, nor put a stumbling block before the blind; but you shall fear your God. I am Yahweh.

Original · Hebrew

לֹא־תְקַלֵּ֣ל חֵרֵ֔שׁ וְלִפְנֵ֣י עִוֵּ֔ר לֹ֥א תִתֵּ֖ן מִכְשֹׁ֑ל וְיָרֵ֥אתָ מֵּאֱלֹהֶ֖יךָ אֲנִ֥י יְהוָֽה׃

the Torah (Leviticus) · 19:14

World English Bible

If a man seeking standing had written this book, the first thing he would cut is a scene where he seems taken up with a man who feels no need, and turns from a blind man. Instead the text tells the scene, corrects it, and is recited still. It does not behave like a self-written biography. That alone does not prove its source. It does make the theory of a forgery for his own benefit harder to hold.

A question for you

Which explanation seems closest to why these verses remain?

If you sayThe speaker is not writing for himself.
ThenThat is where these verses push, and the source of the text remains for you to weigh.
If you sayA clever way to win trust.
ThenThat is possible, and a real objection. Compare its cost with its gain; the next part gives another case.
If you sayI do not know.
ThenThat is fine. For now it is enough to notice that the scene was not hidden.

Part 2 of 3

﴿عَفَا ٱللَّهُ عَنكَ لِمَ أَذِنتَ لَهُمْ حَتَّىٰ يَتَبَيَّنَ لَكَ ٱلَّذِينَ صَدَقُوا۟ وَتَعْلَمَ ٱلْكَـٰذِبِينَ﴾

Translation of the meaning

Allāh has pardoned you, [O Muḥammad, but] why did you give them permission [to remain behind]? [You should not have] until it was evident to you who were truthful and you knew [who were] the liars.

Quran · At-Tawbah 9:43

This verse reviews a decision a leader made before his people: why did you give them leave before the truthful could be told from the false? And its first word is pardon, so the correction opens with forgiveness. This is no book justifying its speaker, and no book humiliating him. It speaks from above him and keeps his dignity at the same time, which is a strange thing for a man writing for himself.

A question for you

Compare the two passages. What do you notice about how the correction is made?

If you sayGentleness with firmness.
ThenThen the speaker in the text treats the man as a dear servant, neither as a master nor as a suspect.
If you sayAn unusual openness.
ThenThat openness is what leaves you asking about the source.
If you sayThat these are few beside the praise.
ThenA fair observation, and the book still kept these few.

Part 3 of 3

﴿قُلْ إِنَّمَآ أَنَا۠ بَشَرٌ مِّثْلُكُمْ يُوحَىٰٓ إِلَىَّ أَنَّمَآ إِلَـٰهُكُمْ إِلَـٰهٌ وَٰحِدٌ ۖ فَمَن كَانَ يَرْجُوا۟ لِقَآءَ رَبِّهِۦ فَلْيَعْمَلْ عَمَلًا صَـٰلِحًا وَلَا يُشْرِكْ بِعِبَادَةِ رَبِّهِۦٓ أَحَدًۢا﴾

Translation of the meaning

Say, "I am only a man like you, to whom has been revealed that your god is one God. So whoever would hope for the meeting with his Lord - let him do righteous work and not associate in the worship of his Lord anyone."

Quran · Al-Kahf 18:110

Translation

When Peter entered, Cornelius met him, fell down at his feet, and worshiped him. But Peter raised him up, saying, “Stand up! I myself am also a man.”

Original · Ancient Greek

ὡς δὲ ἐγένετο τοῦ εἰσελθεῖν τὸν Πέτρον, συναντήσας αὐτῷ ὁ Κορνήλιος πεσὼν ἐπὶ τοὺς πόδας προσεκύνησεν. ὁ δὲ Πέτρος ἤγειρεν αὐτὸν λέγων· Ἀνάστηθι· καὶ ἐγὼ αὐτὸς ἄνθρωπός εἰμι.

Acts · 10:25-26

World English Bible

Why does any of this matter? Because love for a teacher can grow past its place. Had the man appeared flawless, love for him might have grown that way. The text blocks that road with one sentence: I am a human like you. Correcting him protects the meaning of his message: that worship is for God alone. The more human he appears, the clearer it is that the message is about the One who sent him.

A question for you

What does the text protect when it reminds us the man is human?

If you sayThe worship of God alone.
ThenThen the correction is part of the message, and no embarrassment to it.
If you sayPeople's trust in him.
ThenIt may do that too. Compare what that gains with what it leaves behind.
If you sayI do not see that it protects anything.
ThenThen it may help first to say what you would look for in a real message.

The same in the other books
